# Nanolaba logger (Nanolog)

**Nanolog** is a tiny logging facade for Java 8+: every call goes through the static
methods of `LOG`, the source class is detected automatically, so no class needs
a logger field. It works on its own through `ConsoleLogger` or on top of
**SLF4J**, and therefore on top of Logback, Log4j 2, JBoss Logging and others.

## Why Nanolog

- **No logger fields.** `LOG.info("...")` works from any class; the caller is found by walking the stack.
- **Lazy messages.** `LOG.debug(() -> ...)` is evaluated only when the level is enabled.
- **SLF4J-style placeholders.** `{}` with escaping, array rendering and sane handling of missing or extra arguments.
- **Logging never throws.** A broken `toString()` becomes `[FAILED toString()]` instead of an exception in your code.
- **Zero dependencies.** Nine classes, no transitive libraries; `slf4j-api` is needed only if you use `Slf4jLogger`.
- **Pluggable.** A custom backend is one lambda or one class implementing `ILogger`.
- **Fits the agent loop.** One line per log call, output from the first run, an API that fits in one context window; see [Agent-driven development](#agent-driven-development).

The whole library:

```
logging
├── CompositeLogger.java
├── ConsoleLogger.java
├── DefaultLoggerCreator.java
├── ILogger.java
├── JsonLogger.java
├── LOG.java
├── LogEntry.java
├── MemoryLogger.java
├── Slf4jLogger.java
└── package-info.java
```

- `LOG` — the static entry point with all the `trace` / `debug` / `info` / `warn` / `error` overloads.
- `ILogger` — the extension point: one abstract method plus an optional level filter.
- `LogEntry` — one log record and the message formatter.
- `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger`, `Slf4jLogger` — the bundled implementations: text, JSON lines and the bridge to SLF4J.
- `MemoryLogger`, `CompositeLogger` — capturing entries in tests and sending them to several loggers.
- `DefaultLoggerCreator` — picks the logger at startup from a system property or a properties file.

The latest stable version is **1.2**; the version under development is **1.3-SNAPSHOT** (see [Changelog](#changelog)).

## Installation

**Maven (pom.xml)**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.nanolaba</groupId>
    <artifactId>nanolog</artifactId>
    <version>1.2</version>
</dependency>
```

**Gradle (build.gradle)**

```groovy
dependencies {
    implementation 'com.nanolaba:nanolog:1.2'
}
```

<details>
<summary>Manual download</summary>

Get the JAR from [Maven Central](https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/nanolaba/nanolog/1.2) and add it to the classpath.

</details>

Requirements: Java 8+. The jar declares `Automatic-Module-Name: com.nanolaba.nanolog` for modular applications.

## Quick start

No setup is needed: `ConsoleLogger` is active by default and prints every level, including `TRACE`.

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    // No logger field: the source class is detected automatically
    LOG.info("Application started");

    // SLF4J-style {} placeholders
    LOG.debug("Loaded {} items in {} ms", 42, 17);

    // Lazy message: the lambda runs only if DEBUG is enabled
    LOG.debug(() -> "Expensive report: " + buildReport());

    // The source class can also be passed explicitly
    LOG.warn(QuickStart.class, "Disk space is low");

    String input = "not a number";
    try {
        Integer.parseInt(input);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        // Exception plus a parameterized message; the stack trace follows the message
        LOG.error(e, "Failed to parse \"{}\"", input);
    }
}
```

Console output (`ERROR` goes to `System.err`, everything else to `System.out`):

```
INFO 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Application started
DEBUG 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Loaded 42 items in 17 ms
DEBUG 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Expensive report: ...
WARN 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Disk space is low
ERROR 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Failed to parse "not a number"
java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "not a number"
	at java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:65)
	...
```

### API at a glance

Every level has the same set of overloads; `info` below stands for `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.

| Call | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LOG.info(message)` | any object; its `toString()` is called safely |
| `LOG.info("... {} ...", args)` | parameterized message, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting) |
| `LOG.info(() -> message)` | lazy message, evaluated only if the level is enabled |
| `LOG.info(throwable)` | stack trace without a message |
| `LOG.info(throwable, message)` | message plus stack trace; the message may also be a `Supplier` |
| `LOG.info(throwable, "... {} ...", args)` | exception plus a parameterized message |
| `LOG.info("... {} ...", args, throwable)` | the SLF4J order: a trailing exception that no `{}` consumes becomes the exception of the entry |
| `LOG.info(SomeClass.class, ...)` | any form above with an explicit source class |
| `LOG.isInfoEnabled()` | level check, with or without an explicit class |
| `LOG.log(level, sourceClass, throwable, supplier, args)` | the universal entry point every overload delegates to |

Every class and method is documented in the [Javadoc](https://javadoc.io/doc/com.nanolaba/nanolog/1.2), which IDEs also show from the sources jar.

## Agent-driven development

When a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and others) writes and debugs the code,
one short loop repeats many times: edit, run, read the output, edit again.
**Nanolog** keeps every step of that loop cheap.

- **One line to add logging.** No logger field and no `getLogger(Foo.class)` that has to match the class name: one import and `LOG.info(...)`. The diff is a single line, and nothing goes stale when the code is moved or the class is renamed.
- **Output from the first run.** `ConsoleLogger` works without configuration and prints every level, `TRACE` included. A `LOG.debug(...)` added while investigating a problem is visible in the very next run, with no backend to set up first.
- **Levels per run, without code.** `NANOLOG_LEVEL=INFO` cuts the noise once the first run is read, and `-Dnanolog.level.com.acme.payments=DEBUG` turns detail up for one package, even if the startup code switched `DEBUG` off. Agents in sandboxes and CI can always set an environment variable; a temporary code edit, by contrast, tends to get committed. See [Levels and options without code](#levels-and-options-without-code).
- **Lines that are easy to read back.** One entry is one line of the form `LEVEL date [SourceClass] message`, followed by the stack trace if there is one. The output is simple to `grep` and to match against the sources. With `setShowLocation(true)` every line also names the method and the line of the call, `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`, so the agent jumps from the output straight to the statement. Through SLF4J, the backend's own `%file:%line` reports the same call site.
- **Output a script can parse.** `-Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JsonLogger` switches to one JSON object per line, with the timestamp, thread, call site and stack trace as fields, ready for `jq` or a script the agent writes on the fly. See [JsonLogger](#jsonlogger).
- **SLF4J habits carry over.** The same `{}` placeholders, and the exception may go first or last: `LOG.error("Failed to load {}", id, e)` logs the stack trace exactly as SLF4J does.
- **A log call cannot fail the run.** Logging never throws: a broken `toString()`, a `null` or a wrong number of `{}` arguments ends up as a readable message, not as an exception. A log statement is never the reason a test turns red. In test runs, `-Dnanolog.strict=true` still reports such mismatches with the call site, so they get fixed instead of staying silent.
- **The whole library fits in a context window.** Nine small classes, one entry point, this README and the [Javadoc](https://javadoc.io/doc/com.nanolaba/nanolog/1.2). Every public method has Javadoc, so the IDE and the sources jar give the same answers as this file. An agent reads everything it needs in one pass and does not have to map a framework first.
- **Capturing the log in a test takes one line.** `try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install())` keeps the entries in memory and puts the previous logger back afterwards, so what was logged is asserted without a mocking framework; see [MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger](#memorylogger-and-compositelogger).
- **The repository itself is ready for agents.** [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) describes the build, the invariants and the test requirements (JUnit plus 100% mutation coverage), so an agent can fix and extend **Nanolog**, not only use it.

Two files give an agent the rules of the library in a few hundred lines, without the explanations of this README:

## Choosing a logger

The default `ConsoleLogger` can be replaced in three ways:

1. **Programmatically** — pass any `ILogger` implementation to `LOG.init(...)` at application startup:

   ```java
   LOG.init(new Slf4jLogger());
   ```

2. **Via a system property** — the fully qualified name of a class with a public no-arg constructor:

   ```
   -Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.Slf4jLogger
   ```

3. **Via a configuration file** — put `nanolog.properties` on the classpath:

   ```properties
   nanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.Slf4jLogger
   ```

   When `LOG` initialises, the keys of the file with the `nanolog.` prefix are copied
   into system properties without overwriting the ones already set via `-D` or an environment variable.
   Other keys are ignored. The file path can be overridden with the `nanolog.config` property.

Every property can also be set as an environment variable: upper case, dots replaced by underscores, so `nanolog.logger` becomes `NANOLOG_LOGGER`.
Precedence, highest first: `LOG.init(logger)` → `-Dnanolog.logger` → `NANOLOG_LOGGER` → `nanolog.properties` → `ConsoleLogger`.
A no-argument `LOG.init()` re-reads the property and the file.

| Property | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `nanolog.logger` | class name of the `ILogger` implementation | `com.nanolaba.logging.ConsoleLogger` |
| `nanolog.config` | classpath resource with the configuration | `nanolog.properties` |
| `nanolog.strict` | report calls whose `{}` placeholders and arguments do not match, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting) | `false` |

If the class named in `nanolog.logger` cannot be instantiated, **Nanolog** prints a
`[NANOLOG]`-prefixed diagnostic to `System.err` and carries on with `ConsoleLogger`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `LOG.init` replaces the logger for the whole JVM. Call it once at application startup, before other threads start logging. Any library on the classpath can call it as well, so do not call it from library code.

### ConsoleLogger

The default implementation. Writes `ERROR` to `System.err` and everything else to `System.out`, one line per entry plus the stack trace:

```
LEVEL dd.MM.yyyy HH:mm:ss [SourceClass] Message
```

Every component is controlled by a fluent setter:

```java
LOG.init(new ConsoleLogger()
        .setShowLevel(true)
        .setShowDate(true)
        .setDateFormat(new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS"))
        .setShowSource(true)
        .setShowSourceFullName(false)
        .setShowLocation(false)
        .setTraceEnabled(false)
        .setDebugEnabled(false));
```

- `showLevel` — the level name.
- `showDate` + `dateFormat` — the timestamp and its `SimpleDateFormat`; formatting is synchronized, so one shared format is safe.
- `showSource` / `showSourceFullName` — the simple or the fully qualified source class name.
- `showLocation` — the call site after the class name, in the form stack traces use, so IDEs and terminals turn it into a link: `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`. Off by default. A call with an explicit source class has no call site and keeps the plain `[PaymentService]`.
- `traceEnabled` … `errorEnabled` — per-level switches; everything is enabled by default, so switch `TRACE` and `DEBUG` off in production, in code or with `nanolog.level=INFO`. Disabled levels are rejected before the `LogEntry` is built, so lazy messages are never evaluated.

For a custom layout (colours, JSON, a different order) extend `ConsoleLogger` and
override `getOutputStream`, `writeLevel`, `writeDate`, `writeSource`, `writeMessage`,
`writeThrowable` or `addDelimiter`.

### Levels and options without code

The constructor of `ConsoleLogger` reads these settings from system properties, environment variables and `nanolog.properties`, in this order of precedence:

| Property | Environment variable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nanolog.level` | `NANOLOG_LEVEL` | the lowest enabled level: `TRACE` (default), `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, `OFF` |
| `nanolog.level.<package or class>` | — | the level for one package or class |
| `nanolog.levels` | `NANOLOG_LEVELS` | several such rules in one value: `com.acme.payments=DEBUG,com.acme.db=TRACE` |
| `nanolog.console.showLevel` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWLEVEL` | `true` or `false`, like the setter |
| `nanolog.console.showDate` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWDATE` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showSource` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWSOURCE` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showSourceFullName` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWSOURCEFULLNAME` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showLocation` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWLOCATION` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.dateFormat` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_DATEFORMAT` | a `SimpleDateFormat` pattern |

```
java -Dnanolog.level=WARN -Dnanolog.level.com.acme.payments=DEBUG -jar app.jar
NANOLOG_LEVEL=WARN NANOLOG_LEVELS=com.acme.payments=DEBUG java -jar app.jar
```

- A package or class rule beats the global level, however that level was set, setters included. Turning `DEBUG` on for one package therefore needs no code change.
- The most specific rule wins: the class itself, then its enclosing classes, then its packages from the innermost outwards. A rule matches whole name segments only, so `com.acme.pay` does not cover `com.acme.payments`.
- `nanolog.level.<name>` beats an item for the same name in `nanolog.levels`.
- Setters called after the constructor override the values it read, so `new ConsoleLogger().setDebugEnabled(false)` in code wins over `nanolog.level`; package and class rules still apply on top.
- An invalid value prints a `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic to `System.err` and is ignored; logging goes on.
- `nanolog.properties` is read when `LOG` initialises, so a `ConsoleLogger` created before that sees only `-D` and the environment.

### JsonLogger

One JSON object per line, for `jq`, log collectors and scripts. It needs no JSON library and is selected without code:

```
-Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JsonLogger
```

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-11T02:30:31.412Z","level":"WARN","logger":"com.acme.PaymentService","thread":"main","message":"Charge of 42 failed, retrying","template":"Charge of {} failed, retrying","args":["42"],"caller":{"class":"com.acme.PaymentService","method":"charge","file":"PaymentService.java","line":87}}
```

- `ts` — ISO-8601 in UTC with milliseconds, sortable as text; `level`, `logger` (the source class), `thread`, `message` (the formatted message).
- `template` and `args` — the raw message and the arguments as strings, for parameterized messages only; equal events can be grouped whatever their arguments.
- `caller` — the call site, when the source class was detected; `exception` — `class`, `message` and `stackTrace`, when there is a throwable. Fields without a value are left out.
- Line breaks and control characters are escaped, so one entry is always exactly one line, stack trace included.
- `JsonLogger` extends `ConsoleLogger`: the same levels, the same level properties and the same streams (`ERROR` to `System.err`). The display options do not apply.

### Slf4jLogger

The bridge to **SLF4J**. Each entry is forwarded to the `org.slf4j.Logger` named after the source class, so your SLF4J backend sees the real caller, not `LOG`. Levels, patterns, appenders and files are configured in that backend as usual.

> [!NOTE]
> `slf4j-api` is a `provided` dependency of Nanolog. Add it and a backend to your project yourself.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
    <version>2.0.12</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
    <version>1.5.38</version>
</dependency>
```

```java
LOG.init(new Slf4jLogger());
```

Things to know:

- Location-aware backends, Logback and Log4j 2 among them, are told that the call site is the first frame after `LOG`. Their own `%file:%line`, `%method` and `%class` (Logback) or `%l` (Log4j 2) therefore show the code that called `LOG`, not `Slf4jLogger`, with no backend configuration. slf4j-simple prints no location at all.
- The message reaches SLF4J already formatted, so the backend does not see the `{}` arguments as structured data. SLF4J markers are not supported; MDC works as usual because the backend reads it itself.
- An entry without a message is passed with an empty message, not the word `null`.
- An entry without a source class goes to the SLF4J `ROOT` logger.
- Loggers are cached per source class in a `ConcurrentHashMap` and never evicted, so with dynamic class reloading the cache retains `Class` references.

### MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger

`MemoryLogger` keeps entries in memory for tests. Every level is enabled, so entries are captured whatever the production configuration says, and nothing is printed.

```java
void chargeIsRetried() {
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) { // close() puts the previous logger back
        new PaymentService().charge(42); // the code under test

        assertTrue(log.contains(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.WARN, "Charge of 42 failed, retrying"));
    }
}
```

- `install()` replaces the logger of `LOG` and remembers the previous one; `close()` puts it back, also when the test fails. `installForwarding()` does the same but still passes every entry to the previous logger, so the usual output stays visible.
- `getEntries()`, `getEntries(level)`, `getMessages()`, `contains(level, text)`, `clear()` — snapshots and short assertions; the logger is thread-safe.
- `new MemoryLogger(capacity)` keeps only the newest entries.
- `LOG.init` is JVM-wide, so tests that install a logger must not run in parallel with each other.

`CompositeLogger` sends every entry to several loggers. Each of them receives only the levels it has enabled, and a lazy message is built only if at least one of them wants it:

```java
MemoryLogger memory = new MemoryLogger(1000); // keeps the newest 1000 entries
LOG.init(new CompositeLogger(memory, new ConsoleLogger()));
```

## Message formatting

```java
LOG.info("User {} logged in from {}", "alice", "10.0.0.1");  // User alice logged in from 10.0.0.1
LOG.info("Missing arguments stay as is: {} {}", 1);          // Missing arguments stay as is: 1 {}
LOG.info("Extra arguments are ignored: {}", 1, 2);           // Extra arguments are ignored: 1
LOG.info("Escaped placeholder: \\{} then {}", 1);           // Escaped placeholder: {} then 1
LOG.info("Escaped backslash: \\\\{}", 1);                  // Escaped backslash: \1
LOG.info("Arrays: {} and {}", new int[]{1, 2}, new String[][]{{"a"}, {"b"}}); // Arrays: [1, 2] and [[a], [b]]
LOG.info("Null is fine: {}", (Object) null);                 // Null is fine: null
LOG.info("Broken toString(): {}", new BrokenToString());     // Broken toString(): [FAILED toString()]
LOG.error("Failed to load {}", "order", new IOException("timeout")); // Failed to load order, then the stack trace
LOG.error("Cause: {}", new IOException("timeout"));          // Cause: java.io.IOException: timeout
```

- `{}` is replaced by the next argument; `\{}` is a literal `{}` and consumes no argument; `\\{}` is a literal backslash followed by a substitution.
- A `Throwable` in the last position that no `{}` consumes is not an argument: it becomes the exception of the entry, and its stack trace is logged, as in SLF4J. In `LOG.error("Cause: {}", e)` the placeholder takes the exception, so only `e.toString()` is printed. An exception passed first always wins; a trailing one then stays an ordinary argument.
- Primitive arrays are rendered with `Arrays.toString`, object arrays with `Arrays.deepToString`.
- Every `toString()` is guarded: if it throws, the value becomes `[FAILED toString()]` and nothing propagates to the caller. A throwable whose stack trace cannot be printed becomes `[FAILED printStackTrace()]`.
- The message object itself may be anything, not only a `String`; it is converted with the same guarded `toString()`.

### Checking placeholders in tests

Leniency about `{}` is right in production, but during development it hides mistakes: a dropped argument
leaves no trace in the output at all. With `nanolog.strict=true` (or `NANOLOG_STRICT=true`), every call
with arguments whose number of `{}` placeholders differs from the number of arguments additionally
prints one line with the call site to `System.err`:

```
[NANOLOG] com.acme.PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87): 2 placeholders, 1 argument in "Charge of {} for {}"
```

- The entry itself is logged exactly as without the check, and nothing is thrown.
- Each template is reported once; the 1000 most recent reported templates are remembered.
- Only calls with arguments and enabled levels are checked. Escaped `\{}` does not count, and a trailing exception taken as the exception of the entry is not an argument.
- When the check is off, it costs one boolean test per call. The setting is read by `LOG.init()`.

Turn it on for test runs, so mismatches show up in the output that is read anyway:

```xml
<plugin>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <systemPropertyVariables>
            <nanolog.strict>true</nanolog.strict>
        </systemPropertyVariables>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

```groovy
test {
    systemProperty 'nanolog.strict', 'true'
}
```

## Caller detection

When no class is passed explicitly, `LOG` creates a `Throwable`, walks its stack trace
and takes the first frame that does not belong to `LOG`, `LogEntry` or an `ILogger` implementation.

- Nested, anonymous and lambda classes are attributed to their top-level enclosing class.
- The frame found by the walk is kept as `LogEntry.getCaller()`: the exact class, method, file and line of the call, including nested classes and lambdas. It costs nothing extra, and it is `null` when the class was passed explicitly.
- Frame classes are resolved through the context class loader of the thread first and the class loader of `LOG` second, so the detection works when Nanolog lives in a shared loader of an application server and the caller in a web application. A frame neither loader can see is skipped.
- The stack walk happens on every call without an explicit class, including `LOG.isDebugEnabled()`. In hot paths pass the class explicitly: `LOG.debug(MyClass.class, ...)`.
- Any class implementing `ILogger` is skipped, so a custom logger that logs through `LOG` must pass its source class explicitly.

## Writing your own logger

`ILogger` has a single abstract method, so the simplest implementation is a lambda:

```java
LOG.init(entry -> System.out.println(
        entry.getLevel() + " [" + entry.getSourceClass().getSimpleName() + "] " + entry.getFormattedMessage()));
```

A full implementation also filters levels:

```java
public class CustomLogger implements ILogger {

    @Override
    public void log(LogEntry entry) {
        // write the entry wherever you need: a file, a socket, a queue, ...
        System.out.println(entry.getLevel() + " " + entry.getFormattedMessage());
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isEnabled(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel level, Class sourceClass) {
        // called before the LogEntry is built and before any Supplier is evaluated:
        // return false to suppress entries of this level for this class
        return level != LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.TRACE;
    }
}
```

What a `LogEntry` carries:

- `getLevel()` — `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN` or `ERROR`.
- `getSourceClass()` — the detected or explicitly passed class; `null` only if `null` was passed.
- `getCaller()` — the `StackTraceElement` of the logging call; `null` when the source class was passed explicitly.
- `getThrowable()` — the exception or `null`.
- `getMessage()` — the raw message object, already resolved from its `Supplier`.
- `getTimestamp()`, `getThreadName()` — when and in which thread the entry was created, so a logger that writes later or elsewhere still knows.
- `getArgs()` — the substitution arguments.
- `getFormattedMessage()` — the final string with `{}` substituted.

`isEnabled(...)` is called before the `LogEntry` is built and before any `Supplier` is resolved, so returning `false` skips the whole cost of the message.

## Thread safety and performance

- The static `LOG` methods are safe to call from any thread as long as the installed `ILogger` is; `ConsoleLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` are.
- `LOG.init(...)` and the `ConsoleLogger` setters are meant for startup, not for concurrent reconfiguration.
- A call with a disabled level costs one `isEnabled` check plus, without an explicit class, one stack walk. Message formatting and `Supplier` evaluation happen only for enabled levels.

## Using SNAPSHOT versions

Development builds are published to the Sonatype snapshot repository. Add it and depend on the `-SNAPSHOT` version:

**Maven (pom.xml)**

```xml
<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>central.sonatype.com-snapshot</id>
        <url>https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots</url>
        <snapshots>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
            <updatePolicy>always</updatePolicy>
        </snapshots>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.nanolaba</groupId>
    <artifactId>nanolog</artifactId>
    <version>1.3-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
```

**Gradle (build.gradle)**

```groovy
repositories {
    maven {
        url 'https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots'
    }
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'com.nanolaba:nanolog:1.3-SNAPSHOT'
}
```

## Changelog

### 1.3-SNAPSHOT

In development, not released yet.

### 1.2

- A trailing `Throwable` that no `{}` consumes becomes the exception of the entry, as in SLF4J: `LOG.error("Failed", e)` and `LOG.error("Failed {}", id, e)` no longer drop the stack trace.
- `LogEntry.getCaller()` returns the frame of the logging call, and `ConsoleLogger.setShowLocation(true)` prints it as `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`.
- `ConsoleLogger` reads its levels and options from properties and environment variables: `nanolog.level`, `nanolog.level.<package or class>`, `nanolog.levels` and `nanolog.console.*`. Every property, `nanolog.logger` and `nanolog.config` included, can be set as an environment variable (`NANOLOG_LEVEL`), which beats `nanolog.properties`.
- `JsonLogger` writes one JSON object per line. `LogEntry.getTimestamp()` and `LogEntry.getThreadName()` tell when and where an entry was created.
- `MemoryLogger` captures entries in tests (`try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) { ... }`), `CompositeLogger` sends entries to several loggers.
- `nanolog.strict=true` reports calls whose `{}` placeholders and arguments do not match, once per template, with the call site.
- `Slf4jLogger`: location-aware backends (Logback, Log4j 2) report the code that called `LOG` in `%file:%line` and `%l`, instead of `Slf4jLogger.log`.
- `ConsoleLogger`: a throwable whose `toString()` throws no longer escapes from the logging call; it is printed as `[FAILED printStackTrace()]`.
- The whole public API has Javadoc, and the build fails on a missing comment.
- [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) and the agent skill [`skills/nanolog/SKILL.md`](skills/nanolog/SKILL.md) give coding agents the rules of the library; both are generated with the README.

### 1.1

- New overloads `LOG.info(throwable, "... {} ...", args)` and `LOG.info(sourceClass, throwable, "... {} ...", args)` for every level: an exception together with a parameterized message.
- `nanolog.properties`: only `nanolog.` keys are copied into system properties; other keys are ignored.
- `Slf4jLogger`: a `null` source class goes to the `ROOT` logger instead of throwing; an entry without a message no longer logs the word `null`.
- Caller detection resolves classes through the context class loader first and skips frames it cannot see, instead of failing in application servers and plugin frameworks.
- `ConsoleLogger`: timestamp formatting is thread-safe.
- A broken `toString()` inside an `Object[]` argument no longer propagates to the caller.
- A `null` context class loader at startup is tolerated.
- The diagnostic for a missing configuration file names the right property.
- The jar declares `Automatic-Module-Name: com.nanolaba.nanolog`.

### 1.0

First release.

## Contributing

> `README.md` and `README.ru.md` are generated from `README.src.md` by the readme-generator Maven plugin. Edit `README.src.md` and run `mvn compile`; CI fails when the generated files are stale.

- Build and test: `mvn verify -Dgpg.skip=true`. The `test` phase runs JUnit and then pitest with a 100% mutation threshold, so every change to production code needs tests that kill the corresponding mutants.
